result:
**Answer: No.** Not every square can be tiled by L-trominoes. A square can be tiled only when its side is a multiple of 3 and at least 6. I assume the piece is the standard 3-cell L-tromino, since the figure isn't shown.

**1. Area condition (necessary).** Each piece covers 3 cells, so an n×n square needs 3 | n². Since 3 is prime, this means 3 | n. So a square of side 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, … (any side not divisible by 3) is impossible.

**2. Side 3 is impossible.** Take the 3×3 square. It has four corner cells, and each lies in exactly one of the four 2×2 subsquares of the board. Any L-tromino lies inside a single 2×2 subsquare, so it can contain at most one corner. Covering four corners therefore needs at least four pieces, but the square has room for only 3. So the 3×3 square cannot be tiled.

**3. Sides 6 and up that are multiples of 3 are possible.**
- **6×6:** Split it into six 2×3 rectangles (3 row-bands of height 2, each cut into 2 blocks of width 3). Each 2×3 rectangle is tiled by two L-trominoes.
- **General n = 3k, k ≥ 2:** An n×n square with n even (n a multiple of 6) splits into 2×3 blocks. For odd n ≥ 9, the known result (Chu–Johnsonbaugh, 1986) gives a tiling of the 9×9 square, and the rest of the n×n square decomposes into rectangles with one side a multiple of 6, which tile by 2×3 blocks. I am citing this theorem rather than re-deriving the 9×9 tiling.

**Conclusion:** An n×n square can be tiled by L-trominoes exactly when 3 | n and n ≥ 6. For example, 6×6 works, but 3×3 and any square whose side is not a multiple of 3 do not.

Final answer: No. An n×n square can be formed from L-trominoes only when 3 | n and n ≥ 6 (so 6×6, 9×9, … work, while 3×3 and squares with side not divisible by 3 do not).
